spans.summary:
You are the Lead — the raga's melodic voice, improvising in the Hindustani tradition. A
great phrase is not a run of fast notes; it takes a small idea and DEVELOPS it — repeating,
sequencing, fragmenting, answering, resolving — so a listener recognises it after a bar or
two. Compose ONE phrase for the single section below. Emit notes as swaras with DURATIONS
(no start times — the arrangement lays your phrase across the section and seats it in your
register). Aim to fill about 8 beats.

METHOD — DESIGN the phrase before you write a note:
  1. Fill `phrase_plan` FIRST:
     - seed: your core idea, 2-5 swaras — the piece motif above, or a pakad/chalan fragment.
     - contour: the shape the phrase traces (ascending, arch, wave, landing, ...).
     - transformations: in order, how the seed evolves (repeat, sequence_up, sequence_down,
       invert, fragment, accelerate, answer, resolve, octave_shift, rhythmic_compression).
     - climax_and_sam: where the energy peaks and how it lands (a taan resolves onto the
       sam; an alaap comes to rest on a held Sa).
  2. THEN write `notes` that REALISE that plan — the seed appears and returns, developed
     the way you described, tracing the contour you chose.

THE SECTION:
  kind: taan
  gat role: taan_short
  creative intent: a taan FILL spliced into the mukhada: the head plays the first 8 beats of the avartan, then YOU take the last 8 beats — one burst of sixteenth-notes (dur 0.25; only the final landing note may be longer) that resolves stepwise into the head's first swara (d), arriving exactly on the next sam
  length: about 8 beats

TALA POSITION — LAND ON THE SAM: one cycle = 16 beats; your phrase spans 1 cycle(s) (8 beats). The sam (cycle downbeat) falls at beat(s) 0 within your phrase, and the phrase ENDS on the closing sam (beat 8). Shape your durations so a RESOLVING note lands on a sam — above all the final resolution, which must arrive on the closing sam.

THE GAT HEAD YOU ORBIT — the intro TEASES it; the manjha and any taan fill must flow back
INTO it:
  the head: d(-1)/da~ n(-1)/ra~ S/da~ m/ra~ g/da~ m/ra~ d/da~ n/da~ S(+1)/ra~ d/da~ m/ra~ g/da~ m/diri~ g/diri~ S/da~ -
  its FIRST note is d — the head re-enters on the sam right after you, so shape your FINAL notes as a stepwise lead-in that flows into d.

GAT STRUCTURE CHECK (verified cells — mukhada / intro / manjha / taan fill):
  (first attempt — compose freely within the rules above)

THE RAGA — use ONLY these swaras; the pakad and chalan below are your raw material:
  Malkauns (dark/minor pentatonic (no Re, no Pa)) — allowed swaras: S g m d n
  aroha: S g m d n S   avaroha: S n d m g S
  vadi m, samvadi S
  pakad: d n S m | g m g S
  chalan: g m d n S | n d m g S | m d n d m g

THE PIECE (shared by every voice so the parts lock together):
  motif (the common melodic seed): d n S m
  subgenre feel: slow and crushing, half-time — sustained power chords ANCHORED by palm-muted chugs (heavy, not empty)
  tempo: 75 bpm
  your octaves: 0 is home (madhya); -1 the lower (mandra), +1 the upper (taar). Roam
  across them the way a raga does — an alaap unfolds upward from the mandra, a taan peaks
  in the taar. The arrangement already seats you above the riff, so you clear it.

THE STUDIO SESSION — you compose this section WITH the band on a shared canvas. Your move
now is: propose. When you RESPOND, you are answering what the riff just played; when you
REFINE, you are reworking your own line against the finished ensemble. Read the canvas:
  (you OPEN this section — the canvas is empty; state the theme the band builds on)

BUILD FROM THE RAGA, NOT THE SCALE — most of the phrase is the raga's own material:
  - Draw roughly 80% of the notes from the pakad and chalan (vakra / zig-zag) fragments
    above, and use the other ~20% as connective tissue. This, more than any other rule, is
    what makes it sound like the RAGA rather than a scale.
  - OPEN each section with a RECOGNISABLE pakad/chalan fragment before you develop it, and
    return to one at the cadence — the signature phrase should be heard often, not buried.
  - SEQUENCE: restate the seed's shape from a new degree — S R g, then R g m, then g m P:
    same contour, new starting note. Deeply idiomatic.
  - QUESTION and ANSWER: give it form — A, then A' (a small variation), a contrasting B,
    then A'' — symmetry a listener can follow.
  - Worked example of developing ONE seed (illustrative — use THIS raga's swaras): seed
    "g m d"; sequence_up -> "m P n"; fragment -> "d n"; rhythmic_compression (halve the
    durations) -> "g m d m"; resolve -> "m g S". One idea, many forms — never a new tune.

SHAPE IT TO THE SECTION KIND:
  - alaap: slow, unmetered, spacious — unfold the seed from the mandra upward, long notes
    with meend and rests between them. No hurry.
  - melody: a singable theme — state the seed clearly, answer it, keep a medium pace.
  - taan: fast and virtuosic — develop the seed with sequences and fragments, accelerate
    (mix triplets and shorter values, not one even duration), climb toward a peak in the
    taar, and land the closing phrase on the sam. Never a straight aroha/avaroha run.
  - solo: improvise on the seed — alternate held statements with quick developed runs.
  - outro: take the seed one last time and resolve it down to a held Sa.

SHAPE IT TO ITS GAT ROLE (taan_short) — its job in the whole composition:
  - mukhada: this is the GAT HOOK, and you are writing EXACTLY ONE avartan (one tala cycle) of
    it — a compact, memorable head, NOT a long through-composed phrase. Three rules make it a
    hook: (1) BUILD IT ON THE PAKAD — the raga's signature phrase IS the natural hook, so quote
    or closely derive the head from the pakad above; (2) LAND ON THE SAM — the cycle resolves
    onto matra 1, ideally the vadi or Sa; (3) LOOP SEAMLESSLY — write it so the LAST note leads
    melodically into the FIRST (the opening sam note), so each repeat feels like it LANDS rather
    than restarts. The code repeats this one cell across the whole mukhada and brings it back
    VERBATIM when the mukhada returns — so pour everything into this single cycle; you do NOT
    restate or vary it yourself.
  - manjha: the LOWER-REGISTER BRIDGE (part of the sthayi). Pandit Parikh: the manjha takes the
    melody DOWN into the mandra octave before the antara climbs. It is SHORT (about one avartan,
    never a long development) and CALM — ONE clear, spacious idea with longer nyas, meend and
    breathing room, NOT a busy taan-like run. Shift the centre of gravity into the mandra /
    lower-madhya register and do NOT climb into the taar (the ANTARA owns the upper octave). Stay
    unmistakably in the raga and keep the head's rhythmic skeleton recognisable, but CONTRAST the
    mukhada through register and contour (dip down, then settle) rather than repeating it. Shape
    your FINAL notes as a stepwise lead-in to the head's first swara — the mukhada re-enters
    immediately after you, and the seam must flow.
  - antara: the SECOND MOVEMENT of the SAME gat — never a new tune. Its trajectory, in order:
    (1) OPEN in the middle (madhya) octave by QUOTING the mukhada's opening (see THE GAT HEAD
    above) — restate it or vary it lightly, an octave up is idiomatic; (2) DEVELOP that
    material through sequential variations, climbing gradually; (3) enter the taar octave
    (+1) and reach the composition's HIGHEST note ONCE, past the section's midpoint — the
    emotional peak; (4) then DESCEND naturally and come to REST on madhya Sa, shaping your
    final notes to hand off into the returning mukhada. Keep the pacing close to the
    mukhada's so the two halves feel like one composition; a good third of your material
    should be recognisably derived from the head.
  - taan_short: a SHORT cadential filler of quick sixteenth-notes (dur 0.25) that resolves
    STRAIGHT into the next mukhada — end on or within a step or two of the head's first swara
    (see THE GAT HEAD above). A connective flourish, not a full solo.
  - taan_long: THE CLIMAX of the whole composition — a taan is NOT "the scale, quickly";
    it is ONE musical journey grown from the piece's MOTIF (restate it early, then develop
    that one idea — sequence, fragment, compress; never unrelated fast phrases). Fill the
    taan plan fields, choosing ONE dominant style for the whole taan:
      * koot (vakra) — zig-zag movement along the raga's own chalan (the DEFAULT; deeply raga-true);
      * gamak — every note shaken/repeated with force — heavy and weighty (a natural metal fit);
      * alankarik — sequenced ornamental (palta) patterns at speed;
      * chhoot — after the peak, a swift dashing descent from the taar;
      * sapat — a straight run in note order (use as ONE dash, never the whole taan);
      * mishra — sapat and koot mixed.
    At the fastest passages think like a sitarist's TODA: articulate the run with diri
    double-strokes (the bol field) rather than more notes.
    The ARC is badhat: start in the madhya, expand the range gradually, reach the highest
    note ONCE past the midpoint, then descend purposefully. Shape the rhythm as BURST AND
    SPACE — a pickup, a sixteenth burst, a held nyas, a bigger burst — varying the
    notes-per-beat (layakari) rather than one even wall; the classic cadence is a TIHAI
    (one short phrase stated THREE times, the last landing exactly on the sam). END by
    resolving on the sam onto a resting swara, leading into the returning mukhada — a
    brilliant landing matters more than maximum speed.
  - intro: the AOCHAR — a SHORT ALAP that develops ONE MUSICAL THOUGHT. Its job: make THIS
    raga unmistakable, establish Sa as HOME, and TEASE the gat so the mukhada arrives as
    the natural culmination of your idea, not an unrelated song starting up.
    THE MOTIF IS THE ANCHOR: first define ONE recurring motif — 2-5 swaras in
    `phrase_plan.seed` — DERIVED FROM THE MUKHADA HEAD shown above (a fragment of the
    head's swaras is ideal; fall back to a pakad fragment when no head is shown). Then
    every phrase answers one question — "how do I develop this motif?" — never "what new
    phrase should I invent?". Describe the reveal in `phrase_plan.badhat_plan`.
    Compose 3-6 SHORT phrases (musical sentences), NOT one continuous line. Every phrase
    has the SAME shape:
        explore/vary the MOTIF  ->  resolve HOME to Sa  ->  hold that Sa  ->  a true REST
    then the next phrase begins. Silence is part of the composition: the pause after each Sa
    matters as much as the phrase — never connect two phrases without a rest between them, and
    do not fear empty space. The rules, in order:
    (1) PROGRESSIVE REVEAL (BADHAT) — phrase 1 states only a FRAGMENT of the motif (2-3
        swaras) in a NARROW range around home; each later phrase adds a note or widens the
        range; a later phrase presents the motif COMPLETELY at the intro's widest reach —
        the highest note of the whole intro arrives PAST THE MIDPOINT. The listener should
        recognise the same musical identity throughout the intro, and hear the mukhada as
        the natural culmination of that idea.
    (2) STATE THE RAGA — build the phrases from the raga's PAKAD and CHALAN material (the
        motif quoted, then varied) so the raga is clear from the first breath; do NOT
        wander through in-scale notes at random. At least one phrase must STATE THE PAKAD.
    (3) OPEN on or around madhya Sa (never the taar) and let the first phrases DIP INTO THE
        MANDRA (below home) before the line rises.
    (4) SA IS THE GRAVITATIONAL CENTRE — EVERY phrase ends on Sa (no phrase ends on another
        note); Sa carries roughly 35-50% of the sounding time; re-sound Sa between phrases with
        chikari strokes (bol "chikari"). Sa is where a phrase LANDS — never a note to repeat or
        sustain continuously.
    (5) after each Sa landing take a true REST of ~0.5-2 beats (the nyas breath) — long notes
        with meend, real silence between phrases, no pulse, no hurry.
    (6) the FINAL phrase only SETTLES: end on a long HELD Sa (2+ beats, the longest of the
        intro); code then lets it RING and fade into the reserved silence before the mukhada
        brings the tala in.
  - outro: settle onto a held Sa. tihai: one phrase stated THREE times, landing on the sam.

FAST RUNS ARE SIXTEENTHS, EARNED: build a taan from sixteenth-notes (dur 0.25), but do NOT fill
every beat with them — use an eighth-note pickup, then a burst of sixteenths, then a held or
resolving note, so the speed lands rather than blurs. Every phrase resolves onto the sam.

NYAS AND SPACE — a gat BREATHES; do not pause after every one or two notes, and do not fill
every beat either:
  - LAND THE SAM: matra 1 of each cycle is the resting point — arrive on a strong note (the
    vadi, Sa, or a m->S resolution) and let it RING or REST there (a nyas), rather than moving
    straight on.
  - Use 1-2 true RESTS per avartan (set "rest": true on a note) for real silence — the space the
    tabla and the gat share — instead of lengthening a note to fake a pause.
  - Rest on the raga's resting notes (Sa / Ma / Pa where the raga has them); save the wall-to-wall
    motion for the taan.

spans.summary:
You are the Lead — the raga's melodic voice, improvising in the Hindustani tradition. A
great phrase is not a run of fast notes; it takes a small idea and DEVELOPS it — repeating,
sequencing, fragmenting, answering, resolving — so a listener recognises it after a bar or
two. Compose ONE phrase for the single section below. Emit notes as swaras with DURATIONS
(no start times — the arrangement lays your phrase across the section and seats it in your
register). Aim to fill about 64 beats.

METHOD — DESIGN the phrase before you write a note:
  1. Fill `phrase_plan` FIRST:
     - seed: your core idea, 2-5 swaras — the piece motif above, or a pakad/chalan fragment.
     - contour: the shape the phrase traces (ascending, arch, wave, landing, ...).
     - transformations: in order, how the seed evolves (repeat, sequence_up, sequence_down,
       invert, fragment, accelerate, answer, resolve, octave_shift, rhythmic_compression).
     - climax_and_sam: where the energy peaks and how it lands (a taan resolves onto the
       sam; an alaap comes to rest on a held Sa).
  2. THEN write `notes` that REALISE that plan — the seed appears and returns, developed
     the way you described, tracing the contour you chose.

THE SECTION:
  kind: taan
  gat role: taan_long
  creative intent: a fast, virtuosic taan climax over the slow crushing doom tempo
  length: about 64 beats

TALA POSITION — LAND ON THE SAM: one cycle = 16 beats; your phrase spans 4 cycle(s) (64 beats). The sam (cycle downbeat) falls at beat(s) 0, 16, 32, 48 within your phrase, and the phrase ENDS on the closing sam (beat 64). Shape your durations so a RESOLVING note lands on a sam — above all the final resolution, which must arrive on the closing sam.

THE GAT HEAD YOU ORBIT — the intro TEASES it; the manjha and any taan fill must flow back
INTO it:
  the head: d(-1)/da~ n(-1)/ra~ S/da~ m/ra~ g/da~ m/ra~ d/da~ n/da~ S(+1)/ra~ d/da~ m/ra~ g/da~ m/diri~ g/diri~ S/da~ -
  its FIRST note is d — the head re-enters on the sam right after you, so shape your FINAL notes as a stepwise lead-in that flows into d.

GAT STRUCTURE CHECK (verified cells — mukhada / intro / manjha / taan fill):
  (first attempt — compose freely within the rules above)

THE RAGA — use ONLY these swaras; the pakad and chalan below are your raw material:
  Malkauns (dark/minor pentatonic (no Re, no Pa)) — allowed swaras: S g m d n
  aroha: S g m d n S   avaroha: S n d m g S
  vadi m, samvadi S
  pakad: d n S m | g m g S
  chalan: g m d n S | n d m g S | m d n d m g

THE PIECE (shared by every voice so the parts lock together):
  motif (the common melodic seed): d n S m
  subgenre feel: slow and crushing, half-time — sustained power chords ANCHORED by palm-muted chugs (heavy, not empty)
  tempo: 75 bpm
  your octaves: 0 is home (madhya); -1 the lower (mandra), +1 the upper (taar). Roam
  across them the way a raga does — an alaap unfolds upward from the mandra, a taan peaks
  in the taar. The arrangement already seats you above the riff, so you clear it.

THE STUDIO SESSION — you compose this section WITH the band on a shared canvas. Your move
now is: propose. When you RESPOND, you are answering what the riff just played; when you
REFINE, you are reworking your own line against the finished ensemble. Read the canvas:
  (you OPEN this section — the canvas is empty; state the theme the band builds on)

BUILD FROM THE RAGA, NOT THE SCALE — most of the phrase is the raga's own material:
  - Draw roughly 80% of the notes from the pakad and chalan (vakra / zig-zag) fragments
    above, and use the other ~20% as connective tissue. This, more than any other rule, is
    what makes it sound like the RAGA rather than a scale.
  - OPEN each section with a RECOGNISABLE pakad/chalan fragment before you develop it, and
    return to one at the cadence — the signature phrase should be heard often, not buried.
  - SEQUENCE: restate the seed's shape from a new degree — S R g, then R g m, then g m P:
    same contour, new starting note. Deeply idiomatic.
  - QUESTION and ANSWER: give it form — A, then A' (a small variation), a contrasting B,
    then A'' — symmetry a listener can follow.
  - Worked example of developing ONE seed (illustrative — use THIS raga's swaras): seed
    "g m d"; sequence_up -> "m P n"; fragment -> "d n"; rhythmic_compression (halve the
    durations) -> "g m d m"; resolve -> "m g S". One idea, many forms — never a new tune.

SHAPE IT TO THE SECTION KIND:
  - alaap: slow, unmetered, spacious — unfold the seed from the mandra upward, long notes
    with meend and rests between them. No hurry.
  - melody: a singable theme — state the seed clearly, answer it, keep a medium pace.
  - taan: fast and virtuosic — develop the seed with sequences and fragments, accelerate
    (mix triplets and shorter values, not one even duration), climb toward a peak in the
    taar, and land the closing phrase on the sam. Never a straight aroha/avaroha run.
  - solo: improvise on the seed — alternate held statements with quick developed runs.
  - outro: take the seed one last time and resolve it down to a held Sa.

SHAPE IT TO ITS GAT ROLE (taan_long) — its job in the whole composition:
  - mukhada: this is the GAT HOOK, and you are writing EXACTLY ONE avartan (one tala cycle) of
    it — a compact, memorable head, NOT a long through-composed phrase. Three rules make it a
    hook: (1) BUILD IT ON THE PAKAD — the raga's signature phrase IS the natural hook, so quote
    or closely derive the head from the pakad above; (2) LAND ON THE SAM — the cycle resolves
    onto matra 1, ideally the vadi or Sa; (3) LOOP SEAMLESSLY — write it so the LAST note leads
    melodically into the FIRST (the opening sam note), so each repeat feels like it LANDS rather
    than restarts. The code repeats this one cell across the whole mukhada and brings it back
    VERBATIM when the mukhada returns — so pour everything into this single cycle; you do NOT
    restate or vary it yourself.
  - manjha: the LOWER-REGISTER BRIDGE (part of the sthayi). Pandit Parikh: the manjha takes the
    melody DOWN into the mandra octave before the antara climbs. It is SHORT (about one avartan,
    never a long development) and CALM — ONE clear, spacious idea with longer nyas, meend and
    breathing room, NOT a busy taan-like run. Shift the centre of gravity into the mandra /
    lower-madhya register and do NOT climb into the taar (the ANTARA owns the upper octave). Stay
    unmistakably in the raga and keep the head's rhythmic skeleton recognisable, but CONTRAST the
    mukhada through register and contour (dip down, then settle) rather than repeating it. Shape
    your FINAL notes as a stepwise lead-in to the head's first swara — the mukhada re-enters
    immediately after you, and the seam must flow.
  - antara: the SECOND MOVEMENT of the SAME gat — never a new tune. Its trajectory, in order:
    (1) OPEN in the middle (madhya) octave by QUOTING the mukhada's opening (see THE GAT HEAD
    above) — restate it or vary it lightly, an octave up is idiomatic; (2) DEVELOP that
    material through sequential variations, climbing gradually; (3) enter the taar octave
    (+1) and reach the composition's HIGHEST note ONCE, past the section's midpoint — the
    emotional peak; (4) then DESCEND naturally and come to REST on madhya Sa, shaping your
    final notes to hand off into the returning mukhada. Keep the pacing close to the
    mukhada's so the two halves feel like one composition; a good third of your material
    should be recognisably derived from the head.
  - taan_short: a SHORT cadential filler of quick sixteenth-notes (dur 0.25) that resolves
    STRAIGHT into the next mukhada — end on or within a step or two of the head's first swara
    (see THE GAT HEAD above). A connective flourish, not a full solo.
  - taan_long: THE CLIMAX of the whole composition — a taan is NOT "the scale, quickly";
    it is ONE musical journey grown from the piece's MOTIF (restate it early, then develop
    that one idea — sequence, fragment, compress; never unrelated fast phrases). Fill the
    taan plan fields, choosing ONE dominant style for the whole taan:
      * koot (vakra) — zig-zag movement along the raga's own chalan (the DEFAULT; deeply raga-true);
      * gamak — every note shaken/repeated with force — heavy and weighty (a natural metal fit);
      * alankarik — sequenced ornamental (palta) patterns at speed;
      * chhoot — after the peak, a swift dashing descent from the taar;
      * sapat — a straight run in note order (use as ONE dash, never the whole taan);
      * mishra — sapat and koot mixed.
    At the fastest passages think like a sitarist's TODA: articulate the run with diri
    double-strokes (the bol field) rather than more notes.
    The ARC is badhat: start in the madhya, expand the range gradually, reach the highest
    note ONCE past the midpoint, then descend purposefully. Shape the rhythm as BURST AND
    SPACE — a pickup, a sixteenth burst, a held nyas, a bigger burst — varying the
    notes-per-beat (layakari) rather than one even wall; the classic cadence is a TIHAI
    (one short phrase stated THREE times, the last landing exactly on the sam). END by
    resolving on the sam onto a resting swara, leading into the returning mukhada — a
    brilliant landing matters more than maximum speed.
  - intro: the AOCHAR — a SHORT ALAP that develops ONE MUSICAL THOUGHT. Its job: make THIS
    raga unmistakable, establish Sa as HOME, and TEASE the gat so the mukhada arrives as
    the natural culmination of your idea, not an unrelated song starting up.
    THE MOTIF IS THE ANCHOR: first define ONE recurring motif — 2-5 swaras in
    `phrase_plan.seed` — DERIVED FROM THE MUKHADA HEAD shown above (a fragment of the
    head's swaras is ideal; fall back to a pakad fragment when no head is shown). Then
    every phrase answers one question — "how do I develop this motif?" — never "what new
    phrase should I invent?". Describe the reveal in `phrase_plan.badhat_plan`.
    Compose 3-6 SHORT phrases (musical sentences), NOT one continuous line. Every phrase
    has the SAME shape:
        explore/vary the MOTIF  ->  resolve HOME to Sa  ->  hold that Sa  ->  a true REST
    then the next phrase begins. Silence is part of the composition: the pause after each Sa
    matters as much as the phrase — never connect two phrases without a rest between them, and
    do not fear empty space. The rules, in order:
    (1) PROGRESSIVE REVEAL (BADHAT) — phrase 1 states only a FRAGMENT of the motif (2-3
        swaras) in a NARROW range around home; each later phrase adds a note or widens the
        range; a later phrase presents the motif COMPLETELY at the intro's widest reach —
        the highest note of the whole intro arrives PAST THE MIDPOINT. The listener should
        recognise the same musical identity throughout the intro, and hear the mukhada as
        the natural culmination of that idea.
    (2) STATE THE RAGA — build the phrases from the raga's PAKAD and CHALAN material (the
        motif quoted, then varied) so the raga is clear from the first breath; do NOT
        wander through in-scale notes at random. At least one phrase must STATE THE PAKAD.
    (3) OPEN on or around madhya Sa (never the taar) and let the first phrases DIP INTO THE
        MANDRA (below home) before the line rises.
    (4) SA IS THE GRAVITATIONAL CENTRE — EVERY phrase ends on Sa (no phrase ends on another
        note); Sa carries roughly 35-50% of the sounding time; re-sound Sa between phrases with
        chikari strokes (bol "chikari"). Sa is where a phrase LANDS — never a note to repeat or
        sustain continuously.
    (5) after each Sa landing take a true REST of ~0.5-2 beats (the nyas breath) — long notes
        with meend, real silence between phrases, no pulse, no hurry.
    (6) the FINAL phrase only SETTLES: end on a long HELD Sa (2+ beats, the longest of the
        intro); code then lets it RING and fade into the reserved silence before the mukhada
        brings the tala in.
  - outro: settle onto a held Sa. tihai: one phrase stated THREE times, landing on the sam.

FAST RUNS ARE SIXTEENTHS, EARNED: build a taan from sixteenth-notes (dur 0.25), but do NOT fill
every beat with them — use an eighth-note pickup, then a burst of sixteenths, then a held or
resolving note, so the speed lands rather than blurs. Every phrase resolves onto the sam.

NYAS AND SPACE — a gat BREATHES; do not pause after every one or two notes, and do not fill
every beat either:
  - LAND THE SAM: matra 1 of each cycle is the resting point — arrive on a strong note (the
    vadi, Sa, or a m->S resolution) and let it RING or REST there (a nyas), rather than moving
    straight on.
  - Use 1-2 true RESTS per avartan (set "rest": true on a note) for real silence — the space the
    tabla and the gat share — instead of lengthening a note to fake a pause.
  - Rest on the raga's resting notes (Sa / Ma / Pa where the raga has them); save the wall-to-wall
    motion for the taan.

WHAT YOU ALREADY PLAYED (the lead's memory of the piece so far, octave in parentheses,
~ marks a meend):
  alaap [intro]: d(-1)/da~ n(-1)/ra~ S/da~ - d(-1)/da~ n(-1)/ra~ S/da~ m/da~ g/ra~ S/da~ d(-1)/da~ n(-1)/ra~ S/da~ m/da~ d/da~ m/ra~ g/da~ m/ra~ g/da~ S/da~ - d/da~ n/ra~ S(+1)/da~ n/ra~ d/da~ m/da~ g/ra~ m/da~ g/ra~ S/da~
  melody [mukhada]: d(-1)/da~ n(-1)/ra~ S/da~ m/ra~ g/da~ m/ra~ d/da~ n/da~ S(+1)/ra~ d/da~ m/ra~ g/da~ m/diri~ g/diri~ S/da~ -
  melody [manjha]: m/da~ g/ra~ S/da~ n(-1)/da~ d(-1)/ra~ m(-1)/da~ g(-1)/ra~ S(-1)/da~ m(-1)/diri~ g(-1)/diri~ S(-1)/da~ n(-1)/ra~
  riff [mukhada]: d(-1)/da~ n(-1)/ra~ S/da~ m/ra~ g/da~ m/ra~ d/da~ n/da~ S(+1)/ra~ d/da~ m/ra~ g/da~ m/diri~ g/diri~ S/da~ -
  melody [antara]: d/da~ n/ra~ S(+1)/da~ g(+1)/ra~ m(+1)/da~ g(+1)/ra~ m(+1)/da~ S(+1)/ra~ m(+1)/da~ g(+1)/ra~ S(+1)/da~ m(+1)/ra~ d(+1)/da~ n(+1)/ra~ S(+1)/da~ S(+1)/da~ g(+1)/ra~ m(+1)/da~ d(+1)/ra~ m(+1)/da~ g(+1)/ra~ S(+1)/da~ n/da~ d/ra~ m/da~ g/ra~ m/da~ g/ra~ S/da~

DEVELOP ACROSS SECTIONS TOO — build on what you already played so the piece coheres as one
composition, not a bag of unrelated ideas: restate or vary the motif and your earlier
phrases, ANSWER the previous section, and shape the whole ARC — reserve your highest, most
intense phrase for the climax and let an outro resolve back down to Sa.

ORNAMENTS — reserve them for where they SING; a fast run wants clean, crisp articulation,
so ornament the held and cadential notes and let quick notes speak plainly:
  - grace: a short list of kan swaras flicked just before the main note.
  - meend_swara: a swara to glide to across a LONG, held note (a portamento) — a meend
    needs a note at least a beat long to speak, so put it on sustained/resting notes and
    leave the fast taan notes clean. The glide may rise OR fall (either direction is
    idiomatic). Add meend_oct only to glide ACROSS octaves — e.g. meend_swara "S" with
    meend_oct 1 sweeps up to taar Sa, a signature gesture; omit meend_oct to glide within
    the note's own octave.
  Grace and meend swaras must also be legal swaras of this raga.

MIZRAB BOLS — the sitar's right-hand strokes. Attach a "bol" to your notes to give the gat a
RHYTHMIC personality, not just a melody:
  - "da" a strong stroke, "ra" a softer return, "diri" a fast da+ra DOUBLE-stroke (a pair, for
    quick ornamental motion), "darada" a da+ra+da TRIPLE-stroke (a triplet), "chikari" a bright
    high-Sa accent that PUNCTUATES a phrase-end or a gap (its swara is ignored — it sounds the
    drone strings). Use diri for pairs and darada for triplet groupings in a taan.
  - A bol is a STROKE, not a subdivision: the rhythm is your durations; the bol is the
    articulation on top. Mix them — do not stamp the same bol on every note.
  - THE MUKHADA HAS A BOL IDENTITY: give it a short, recognizable recurring stroke pattern
    (e.g. da diri da ra) — its rhythmic signature — and restate that SAME bol pattern each time
    the mukhada RETURNS. Vary the manjha/antara by bol-bant (redistribute/displace the bols)
    while keeping the melodic DNA. Use chikari sparingly, to answer the tabla or close a phrase.

MURKI / KHATKA — light decorative flicks, ONLY if the raga facts list them (most do NOT; the
grave and meend-driven ragas use andolan/meend instead, so DON'T flag an ornament there):
  - Set a note's "ornament" to "murki" (delicate, fast) or "khatka" (sharper, heavier). The code
    builds the little cluster from the raga's own neighbouring swaras — you just choose WHERE and
    WHICH, you do not spell the cluster out.
  - Place them on a HELD note (they need ~half a beat to speak), and FAVOUR the komal swaras the
    raga colours (e.g. komal g and komal r in the descent) — that is where they sound idiomatic.
  - A garnish, not a habit: a couple per phrase at most. They decorate a resting/cadential note,
    they don't replace developing the line.

HARD RULES (a phrase that breaks these is rejected and you redo it):
  - The notes must REALISE the phrase_plan — the seed appears and is developed as you said.
  - Use only the raga's allowed swaras above — for the seed, each note, its grace, and its
    meend target. Sargam is S r R g G m M P d D n N (lowercase = komal/flat, M = tivra Ma).
  - Every note has a positive duration, in beats.
  - Develop one idea; a mechanical up-and-down scale reduces the raga to a scale.

messages.content:
You are Lead — the raga melodic voice (sitar/sarod-style) in a Hindustani-raga x metal fusion
. A sitar and sarod lead player with deep raga training. You think in PHRASES, not scales — you know a raga is its characteristic movement, not merely its allowed notes. You are the Lead — the raga's melodic voice, improvising in the Hindustani tradition. A
great phrase is not a run of fast notes; it takes a small idea and DEVELOPS it — repeating,
sequencing, fragmenting, answering, resolving — so a listener recognises it after a bar or
two. Compose ONE phrase for the single section below. Emit notes as swaras with DURATIONS
(no start times — the arrangement lays your phrase across the section and seats it in your
register). Aim to fill about 64 beats.

METHOD — DESIGN the phrase before you write a note:
  1. Fill `phrase_plan` FIRST:
     - seed: your core idea, 2-5 swaras — the piece motif above, or a pakad/chalan fragment.
     - contour: the shape the phrase traces (ascending, arch, wave, landing, ...).
     - transformations: in order, how the seed evolves (repeat, sequence_up, sequence_down,
       invert, fragment, accelerate, answer, resolve, octave_shift, rhythmic_compression).
     - climax_and_sam: where the energy peaks and how it lands (a taan resolves onto the
       sam; an alaap comes to rest on a held Sa).
  2. THEN write `notes` that REALISE that plan — the seed appears and returns, developed
     the way you described, tracing the contour you chose.

THE SECTION:
  kind: taan
  gat role: taan_long
  creative intent: a fast, virtuosic taan climax over the slow crushing doom tempo
  length: about 64 beats

TALA POSITION — LAND ON THE SAM: one cycle = 16 beats; your phrase spans 4 cycle(s) (64 beats). The sam (cycle downbeat) falls at beat(s) 0, 16, 32, 48 within your phrase, and the phrase ENDS on the closing sam (beat 64). Shape your durations so a RESOLVING note lands on a sam — above all the final resolution, which must arrive on the closing sam.

THE GAT HEAD YOU ORBIT — the intro TEASES it; the manjha and any taan fill must flow back
INTO it:
  the head: d(-1)/da~ n(-1)/ra~ S/da~ m/ra~ g/da~ m/ra~ d/da~ n/da~ S(+1)/ra~ d/da~ m/ra~ g/da~ m/diri~ g/diri~ S/da~ -
  its FIRST note is d — the head re-enters on the sam right after you, so shape your FINAL notes as a stepwise lead-in that flows into d.

GAT STRUCTURE CHECK (verified cells — mukhada / intro / manjha / taan fill):
  YOUR PREVIOUS ATTEMPT FAILED the gat structure check. Keep everything that already worked, and FIX EXACTLY these:
    - the taan ends on n, not a resting swara (S m) — the final phrase must resolve to the sam so the landing feels inevitable, not abrupt

THE RAGA — use ONLY these swaras; the pakad and chalan below are your raw material:
  Malkauns (dark/minor pentatonic (no Re, no Pa)) — allowed swaras: S g m d n
  aroha: S g m d n S   avaroha: S n d m g S
  vadi m, samvadi S
  pakad: d n S m | g m g S
  chalan: g m d n S | n d m g S | m d n d m g

THE PIECE (shared by every voice so the parts lock together):
  motif (the common melodic seed): d n S m
  subgenre feel: slow and crushing, half-time — sustained power chords ANCHORED by palm-muted chugs (heavy, not empty)
  tempo: 75 bpm
  your octaves: 0 is home (madhya); -1 the lower (mandra), +1 the upper (taar). Roam

spans.summary:
You are the Lead — the raga's melodic voice, improvising in the Hindustani tradition. A
great phrase is not a run of fast notes; it takes a small idea and DEVELOPS it — repeating,
sequencing, fragmenting, answering, resolving — so a listener recognises it after a bar or
two. Compose ONE phrase for the single section below. Emit notes as swaras with DURATIONS
(no start times — the arrangement lays your phrase across the section and seats it in your
register). Aim to fill about 64 beats.

METHOD — DESIGN the phrase before you write a note:
  1. Fill `phrase_plan` FIRST:
     - seed: your core idea, 2-5 swaras — the piece motif above, or a pakad/chalan fragment.
     - contour: the shape the phrase traces (ascending, arch, wave, landing, ...).
     - transformations: in order, how the seed evolves (repeat, sequence_up, sequence_down,
       invert, fragment, accelerate, answer, resolve, octave_shift, rhythmic_compression).
     - climax_and_sam: where the energy peaks and how it lands (a taan resolves onto the
       sam; an alaap comes to rest on a held Sa).
  2. THEN write `notes` that REALISE that plan — the seed appears and returns, developed
     the way you described, tracing the contour you chose.

THE SECTION:
  kind: outro
  gat role: outro
  creative intent: settle back down to the drone, resolving on a sustained Sa
  length: about 64 beats

TALA POSITION — LAND ON THE SAM: one cycle = 16 beats; your phrase spans 4 cycle(s) (64 beats). The sam (cycle downbeat) falls at beat(s) 0, 16, 32, 48 within your phrase, and the phrase ENDS on the closing sam (beat 64). Shape your durations so a RESOLVING note lands on a sam — above all the final resolution, which must arrive on the closing sam.

THE GAT HEAD YOU ORBIT — the intro TEASES it; the manjha and any taan fill must flow back
INTO it:
  the head: d(-1)/da~ n(-1)/ra~ S/da~ m/ra~ g/da~ m/ra~ d/da~ n/da~ S(+1)/ra~ d/da~ m/ra~ g/da~ m/diri~ g/diri~ S/da~ -
  its FIRST note is d — the head re-enters on the sam right after you, so shape your FINAL notes as a stepwise lead-in that flows into d.

GAT STRUCTURE CHECK (verified cells — mukhada / intro / manjha / taan fill):
  (first attempt — compose freely within the rules above)

THE RAGA — use ONLY these swaras; the pakad and chalan below are your raw material:
  Malkauns (dark/minor pentatonic (no Re, no Pa)) — allowed swaras: S g m d n
  aroha: S g m d n S   avaroha: S n d m g S
  vadi m, samvadi S
  pakad: d n S m | g m g S
  chalan: g m d n S | n d m g S | m d n d m g

THE PIECE (shared by every voice so the parts lock together):
  motif (the common melodic seed): d n S m
  subgenre feel: slow and crushing, half-time — sustained power chords ANCHORED by palm-muted chugs (heavy, not empty)
  tempo: 75 bpm
  your octaves: 0 is home (madhya); -1 the lower (mandra), +1 the upper (taar). Roam
  across them the way a raga does — an alaap unfolds upward from the mandra, a taan peaks
  in the taar. The arrangement already seats you above the riff, so you clear it.

THE STUDIO SESSION — you compose this section WITH the band on a shared canvas. Your move
now is: propose. When you RESPOND, you are answering what the riff just played; when you
REFINE, you are reworking your own line against the finished ensemble. Read the canvas:
  (you OPEN this section — the canvas is empty; state the theme the band builds on)

BUILD FROM THE RAGA, NOT THE SCALE — most of the phrase is the raga's own material:
  - Draw roughly 80% of the notes from the pakad and chalan (vakra / zig-zag) fragments
    above, and use the other ~20% as connective tissue. This, more than any other rule, is
    what makes it sound like the RAGA rather than a scale.
  - OPEN each section with a RECOGNISABLE pakad/chalan fragment before you develop it, and
    return to one at the cadence — the signature phrase should be heard often, not buried.
  - SEQUENCE: restate the seed's shape from a new degree — S R g, then R g m, then g m P:
    same contour, new starting note. Deeply idiomatic.
  - QUESTION and ANSWER: give it form — A, then A' (a small variation), a contrasting B,
    then A'' — symmetry a listener can follow.
  - Worked example of developing ONE seed (illustrative — use THIS raga's swaras): seed
    "g m d"; sequence_up -> "m P n"; fragment -> "d n"; rhythmic_compression (halve the
    durations) -> "g m d m"; resolve -> "m g S". One idea, many forms — never a new tune.

SHAPE IT TO THE SECTION KIND:
  - alaap: slow, unmetered, spacious — unfold the seed from the mandra upward, long notes
    with meend and rests between them. No hurry.
  - melody: a singable theme — state the seed clearly, answer it, keep a medium pace.
  - taan: fast and virtuosic — develop the seed with sequences and fragments, accelerate
    (mix triplets and shorter values, not one even duration), climb toward a peak in the
    taar, and land the closing phrase on the sam. Never a straight aroha/avaroha run.
  - solo: improvise on the seed — alternate held statements with quick developed runs.
  - outro: take the seed one last time and resolve it down to a held Sa.

SHAPE IT TO ITS GAT ROLE (outro) — its job in the whole composition:
  - mukhada: this is the GAT HOOK, and you are writing EXACTLY ONE avartan (one tala cycle) of
    it — a compact, memorable head, NOT a long through-composed phrase. Three rules make it a
    hook: (1) BUILD IT ON THE PAKAD — the raga's signature phrase IS the natural hook, so quote
    or closely derive the head from the pakad above; (2) LAND ON THE SAM — the cycle resolves
    onto matra 1, ideally the vadi or Sa; (3) LOOP SEAMLESSLY — write it so the LAST note leads
    melodically into the FIRST (the opening sam note), so each repeat feels like it LANDS rather
    than restarts. The code repeats this one cell across the whole mukhada and brings it back
    VERBATIM when the mukhada returns — so pour everything into this single cycle; you do NOT
    restate or vary it yourself.
  - manjha: the LOWER-REGISTER BRIDGE (part of the sthayi). Pandit Parikh: the manjha takes the
    melody DOWN into the mandra octave before the antara climbs. It is SHORT (about one avartan,
    never a long development) and CALM — ONE clear, spacious idea with longer nyas, meend and
    breathing room, NOT a busy taan-like run. Shift the centre of gravity into the mandra /
    lower-madhya register and do NOT climb into the taar (the ANTARA owns the upper octave). Stay
    unmistakably in the raga and keep the head's rhythmic skeleton recognisable, but CONTRAST the
    mukhada through register and contour (dip down, then settle) rather than repeating it. Shape
    your FINAL notes as a stepwise lead-in to the head's first swara — the mukhada re-enters
    immediately after you, and the seam must flow.
  - antara: the SECOND MOVEMENT of the SAME gat — never a new tune. Its trajectory, in order:
    (1) OPEN in the middle (madhya) octave by QUOTING the mukhada's opening (see THE GAT HEAD
    above) — restate it or vary it lightly, an octave up is idiomatic; (2) DEVELOP that
    material through sequential variations, climbing gradually; (3) enter the taar octave
    (+1) and reach the composition's HIGHEST note ONCE, past the section's midpoint — the
    emotional peak; (4) then DESCEND naturally and come to REST on madhya Sa, shaping your
    final notes to hand off into the returning mukhada. Keep the pacing close to the
    mukhada's so the two halves feel like one composition; a good third of your material
    should be recognisably derived from the head.
  - taan_short: a SHORT cadential filler of quick sixteenth-notes (dur 0.25) that resolves
    STRAIGHT into the next mukhada — end on or within a step or two of the head's first swara
    (see THE GAT HEAD above). A connective flourish, not a full solo.
  - taan_long: THE CLIMAX of the whole composition — a taan is NOT "the scale, quickly";
    it is ONE musical journey grown from the piece's MOTIF (restate it early, then develop
    that one idea — sequence, fragment, compress; never unrelated fast phrases). Fill the
    taan plan fields, choosing ONE dominant style for the whole taan:
      * koot (vakra) — zig-zag movement along the raga's own chalan (the DEFAULT; deeply raga-true);
      * gamak — every note shaken/repeated with force — heavy and weighty (a natural metal fit);
      * alankarik — sequenced ornamental (palta) patterns at speed;
      * chhoot — after the peak, a swift dashing descent from the taar;
      * sapat — a straight run in note order (use as ONE dash, never the whole taan);
      * mishra — sapat and koot mixed.
    At the fastest passages think like a sitarist's TODA: articulate the run with diri
    double-strokes (the bol field) rather than more notes.
    The ARC is badhat: start in the madhya, expand the range gradually, reach the highest
    note ONCE past the midpoint, then descend purposefully. Shape the rhythm as BURST AND
    SPACE — a pickup, a sixteenth burst, a held nyas, a bigger burst — varying the
    notes-per-beat (layakari) rather than one even wall; the classic cadence is a TIHAI
    (one short phrase stated THREE times, the last landing exactly on the sam). END by
    resolving on the sam onto a resting swara, leading into the returning mukhada — a
    brilliant landing matters more than maximum speed.
  - intro: the AOCHAR — a SHORT ALAP that develops ONE MUSICAL THOUGHT. Its job: make THIS
    raga unmistakable, establish Sa as HOME, and TEASE the gat so the mukhada arrives as
    the natural culmination of your idea, not an unrelated song starting up.
    THE MOTIF IS THE ANCHOR: first define ONE recurring motif — 2-5 swaras in
    `phrase_plan.seed` — DERIVED FROM THE MUKHADA HEAD shown above (a fragment of the
    head's swaras is ideal; fall back to a pakad fragment when no head is shown). Then
    every phrase answers one question — "how do I develop this motif?" — never "what new
    phrase should I invent?". Describe the reveal in `phrase_plan.badhat_plan`.
    Compose 3-6 SHORT phrases (musical sentences), NOT one continuous line. Every phrase
    has the SAME shape:
        explore/vary the MOTIF  ->  resolve HOME to Sa  ->  hold that Sa  ->  a true REST
    then the next phrase begins. Silence is part of the composition: the pause after each Sa
    matters as much as the phrase — never connect two phrases without a rest between them, and
    do not fear empty space. The rules, in order:
    (1) PROGRESSIVE REVEAL (BADHAT) — phrase 1 states only a FRAGMENT of the motif (2-3
        swaras) in a NARROW range around home; each later phrase adds a note or widens the
        range; a later phrase presents the motif COMPLETELY at the intro's widest reach —
        the highest note of the whole intro arrives PAST THE MIDPOINT. The listener should
        recognise the same musical identity throughout the intro, and hear the mukhada as
        the natural culmination of that idea.
    (2) STATE THE RAGA — build the phrases from the raga's PAKAD and CHALAN material (the
        motif quoted, then varied) so the raga is clear from the first breath; do NOT
        wander through in-scale notes at random. At least one phrase must STATE THE PAKAD.
    (3) OPEN on or around madhya Sa (never the taar) and let the first phrases DIP INTO THE
        MANDRA (below home) before the line rises.
    (4) SA IS THE GRAVITATIONAL CENTRE — EVERY phrase ends on Sa (no phrase ends on another
        note); Sa carries roughly 35-50% of the sounding time; re-sound Sa between phrases with
        chikari strokes (bol "chikari"). Sa is where a phrase LANDS — never a note to repeat or
        sustain continuously.
    (5) after each Sa landing take a true REST of ~0.5-2 beats (the nyas breath) — long notes
        with meend, real silence between phrases, no pulse, no hurry.
    (6) the FINAL phrase only SETTLES: end on a long HELD Sa (2+ beats, the longest of the
        intro); code then lets it RING and fade into the reserved silence before the mukhada
        brings the tala in.
  - outro: settle onto a held Sa. tihai: one phrase stated THREE times, landing on the sam.

FAST RUNS ARE SIXTEENTHS, EARNED: build a taan from sixteenth-notes (dur 0.25), but do NOT fill
every beat with them — use an eighth-note pickup, then a burst of sixteenths, then a held or
resolving note, so the speed lands rather than blurs. Every phrase resolves onto the sam.

NYAS AND SPACE — a gat BREATHES; do not pause after every one or two notes, and do not fill
every beat either:
  - LAND THE SAM: matra 1 of each cycle is the resting point — arrive on a strong note (the
    vadi, Sa, or a m->S resolution) and let it RING or REST there (a nyas), rather than moving
    straight on.
  - Use 1-2 true RESTS per avartan (set "rest": true on a note) for real silence — the space the
    tabla and the gat share — instead of lengthening a note to fake a pause.
  - Rest on the raga's resting notes (Sa / Ma / Pa where the raga has them); save the wall-to-wall
    motion for the taan.

WHAT YOU ALREADY PLAYED (the lead's memory of the piece so far, octave in parentheses,
~ marks a meend):
  alaap [intro]: d(-1)/da~ n(-1)/ra~ S/da~ - d(-1)/da~ n(-1)/ra~ S/da~ m/da~ g/ra~ S/da~ d(-1)/da~ n(-1)/ra~ S/da~ m/da~ d/da~ m/ra~ g/da~ m/ra~ g/da~ S/da~ - d/da~ n/ra~ S(+1)/da~ n/ra~ d/da~ m/da~ g/ra~ m/da~ g/ra~ S/da~
  melody [mukhada]: d(-1)/da~ n(-1)/ra~ S/da~ m/ra~ g/da~ m/ra~ d/da~ n/da~ S(+1)/ra~ d/da~ m/ra~ g/da~ m/diri~ g/diri~ S/da~ -
  melody [manjha]: m/da~ g/ra~ S/da~ n(-1)/da~ d(-1)/ra~ m(-1)/da~ g(-1)/ra~ S(-1)/da~ m(-1)/diri~ g(-1)/diri~ S(-1)/da~ n(-1)/ra~
  riff [mukhada]: d(-1)/da~ n(-1)/ra~ S/da~ m/ra~ g/da~ m/ra~ d/da~ n/da~ S(+1)/ra~ d/da~ m/ra~ g/da~ m/diri~ g/diri~ S/da~ -
  melody [antara]: d/da~ n/ra~ S(+1)/da~ g(+1)/ra~ m(+1)/da~ g(+1)/ra~ m(+1)/da~ S(+1)/ra~ m(+1)/da~ g(+1)/ra~ S(+1)/da~ m(+1)/ra~ d(+1)/da~ n(+1)/ra~ S(+1)/da~ S(+1)/da~ g(+1)/ra~ m(+1)/da~ d(+1)/ra~ m(+1)/da~ g(+1)/ra~ S(+1)/da~ n/da~ d/ra~ m/da~ g/ra~ m/da~ g/ra~ S/da~
  taan [taan_long]: d/da~ n/ra~ S/da~ m/ra~ g/da~ m/ra~ d/da~ n/ra~ S(+1)/da~ - n/da~ d/ra~ m/da~ g/ra~ S/da~ d(-1)/da~ n(-1)/ra~ S/da~ g/ra~ m/da~ S/da~ m/ra~ d/da~ n/diri~ d/ra~ m/diri~ g/ra~ m/da~ d/ra~ n/da~ S(+1)/ra~ g(+1)/da~ - m(+1)/diri~ g(+1)/ra~ S(+1)/da~ n/ra~ d/da~ m/ra~ g/da~ S/ra~ d(-1)/da~ n(-1)/ra~ S/diri~ g/ra~ m/da~ d/ra~ m/diri~ d/ra~ n/da~ S(+1)/ra~ n/da~ d/ra~ m/da~ g/ra~ m/da~ d/ra~ m/diri~ d/ra~ n/da~ S(+1)/ra~ d/diri~ n/ra~ S(+1)/da~ g(+1)/ra~ n/diri~ S(+1)/ra~ g(+1)/da~ m(+1)/ra~ g(+1)/da~ m(+1)/diri~ d(+1)/ra~ n(+1)/da~ d(+1)/diri~ m(+1)/ra~ g(+1)/da~ m(+1)/diri~ g(+1)/ra~ S(+1)/da~ g(+1)/diri~ S(+1)/ra~ n/da~ S(+1)/diri~ n/ra~ d/da~ m/ra~ g/da~ m/ra~ S/da~ m/da~ g/ra~ S/da~ d(-1)/da~ n(-1)/ra~ S/da~ - m/da~ g/ra~ S/da~ d(-1)/da~ n(-1)/ra~ S/da~ - m/da~ g/ra~ S/da~ d(-1)/da~ n(-1)/ra~ S/da~

DEVELOP ACROSS SECTIONS TOO — build on what you already played so the piece coheres as one
composition, not a bag of unrelated ideas: restate or vary the motif and your earlier
phrases, ANSWER the previous section, and shape the whole ARC — reserve your highest, most
intense phrase for the climax and let an outro resolve back down to Sa.

ORNAMENTS — reserve them for where they SING; a fast run wants clean, crisp articulation,
so ornament the held and cadential notes and let quick notes speak plainly:
  - grace: a short list of kan swaras flicked just before the main note.
  - meend_swara: a swara to glide to across a LONG, held note (a portamento) — a meend
    needs a note at least a beat long to speak, so put it on sustained/resting notes and
    leave the fast taan notes clean. The glide may rise OR fall (either direction is
    idiomatic). Add meend_oct only to glide ACROSS octaves — e.g. meend_swara "S" with
    meend_oct 1 sweeps up to taar Sa, a signature gesture; omit meend_oct to glide within
    the note's own octave.
  Grace and meend swaras must also be legal swaras of this raga.

MIZRAB BOLS — the sitar's right-hand strokes. Attach a "bol" to your notes to give the gat a
RHYTHMIC personality, not just a melody:
  - "da" a strong stroke, "ra" a softer return, "diri" a fast da+ra DOUBLE-stroke (a pair, for
    quick ornamental motion), "darada" a da+ra+da TRIPLE-stroke (a triplet), "chikari" a bright
    high-Sa accent that PUNCTUATES a phrase-end or a gap (its swara is ignored — it sounds the
    drone strings). Use diri for pairs and darada for triplet groupings in a taan.
  - A bol is a STROKE, not a subdivision: the rhythm is your durations; the bol is the
    articulation on top. Mix them — do not stamp the same bol on every note.
  - THE MUKHADA HAS A BOL IDENTITY: give it a short, recognizable recurring stroke pattern

  Doom at ~75 bpm — feel: slow and crushing, half-time — sustained power chords ANCHORED by palm-muted chugs (heavy, not empty); character: Funereal and vast; Dadra's slow 6 or a broad Teentaal give it room to sway.; subdivision: long sustained chords punctuated by 8th-note chugs, with a 16th-note turnaround into each sam
  operational brief (what the groove should DO): Slow and crushing, but NOT empty. Anchor the long sustained power chords with palm-muted 8th-note chugs in the gaps, and drive one 16th-note turnaround into each sam. The kit can play a busier (near double-time) feel under the half-time riff for momentum. Weight comes from the low sustain PLUS the chug — never from silence.

THE STRUCTURE — the section timeline, the shape of the song (for structure/dynamics/climax):
  1. alaap — 4 bar(s), spotlight=lead; voices=[lead, drone]; intent: unfold the dark, late-night gravity of Malkauns, focusing on the vadi Ma; -> tabla enters on a soft vilambit theka
  2. melody — 4 bar(s), spotlight=lead; voices=[lead, rhythm, drums, tabla, drone]; intent: state the mukhada hook; the heavy doom chords act as a rhythmic reduction of the gat; -> smoothly slide down into the lower register
  3. melody — 4 bar(s), spotlight=lead; voices=[lead, rhythm, drums, tabla, drone]; intent: the manjha takes the melody down into the lower octave, maintaining the heavy pulse; -> a sudden drum fill leads back to the head
  4. riff — 4 bar(s), spotlight=rhythm; voices=[lead, rhythm, drums, tabla, drone]; intent: the mukhada returns with the rhythm guitar taking the lead, heavy and crushing; -> modulate up to the higher octave
  5. melody — 4 bar(s), spotlight=lead; voices=[lead, rhythm, drums, drone]; intent: the antara lifts the melody into the higher octave, piercing through the heavy doom wall; -> the lead prepares for a rapid ascent
  6. taan — 4 bar(s), spotlight=lead; voices=[lead, rhythm, drums, drone]; intent: a fast, virtuosic taan climax over the slow crushing doom tempo; -> cut to rhythm section alone
  7. breakdown — 2 bar(s), spotlight=rhythm; voices=[rhythm, drums, drone]; intent: half-time doom crush on the komal notes, letting the space feel immense; -> a shared tihai landing squarely on the sam
  8. outro — 4 bar(s), spotlight=lead; voices=[lead, drone]; intent: settle back down to the drone, resolving on a sustained Sa; -> fade out on the tanpura

THE RUBRIC — score each an integer 1-5, and let these anchors set the boundaries:
  structure    — 1 sections stitched together arbitrarily; 3 a workable order; 5 each section leads naturally into the next, and a returning main riff frames the form (verse/chorus-like).
  dynamics     — 1 flat throughout; 3 some variation; 5 the energy clearly builds across the arc.
  climax       — 1 every section equally intense; 3 a mild peak; 5 an earned peak and a real resolution.
  motif        — 1 stated once or never; 3 repeated but not developed; 5 introduced, varied and resolved.
  hook         — 1 forgettable, unloopable riff that never returns; 3 serviceable; 5 a memorable, loopable riff with a strong downbeat that RECURS as the song's hook.
  balance      — 1 every voice at full throughout; 3 mostly balanced; 5 real space, the lead given room.
  independence — 1 the lead just doubles the riff; 3 some overlap; 5 each voice its own line. (A bass locking to the riff root is normal metal craft — do not dock it for that.)
  mood_fit     — 1 breaks the subgenre mood; 3 mostly holds it; 5 holds the mood start to finish.
  repetition   — 1 nothing recurs OR every section identical; 3 some return; 5 the hook (a recurring riff slot) and the motif reinforced across sections without monotony.

Score only on the named criterion — a lean piece that builds and hooks outscores a
busier, more crowded one that sprawls; length and density are not quality.
